items.title: Expert Consensus Recommendations on NSCLC Management: Evidence-Based Strategies for Early Resectable and Locally Advanced Disease from Asia
items.authors: Soo RA, Sachithanandan A, Higgins KA, et al.
items.abstract: Lung cancer remains the most common malignancy in Asia and is characterised by a substantial proportion of cases occurring in never-smokers, a feature that distinguishes the region from many Western populations. Only 20-25% of patients with newly diagnosed non‑small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) present with resectable disease. As precision oncology expands into earlier stages, understanding how global standards can be adapted to Asian healthcare systems is increasingly important. This expert consensus report summarises evidence-informed opinions and voting outcomes from 13 lung cancer specialists across 11 countries to identify regional priorities, practical implementation needs, and management strategies for early and locally advanced NSCLC. Experts supported annual low‑dose CT (LDCT) screening for high‑risk individuals, with adaptation of criteria to better capture Asia's substantial burden of never‑smokers and individuals with strong family history. Early diagnostic pathways emphasised rapid tissue acquisition and timely biomarker testing specifically EGFR, ALK, and PD‑L1 at initial diagnosis for both resectable and unresectable disease. Across resectable stage II-III disease, evidence from multiple Phase III trials consistently demonstrates that integrating immunotherapy with neoadjuvant or perioperative chemotherapy improves pathological response and event‑free survival, while maintaining surgical feasibility. Differences between regimens relate largely to timing, agent selection, and biomarker effects, and practical adoption in Asia varies according to diagnostic capacity and local resource availability. For unresectable stage III NSCLC, concurrent chemoradiotherapy followed by consolidation durvalumab remains standard, while recent data from the LAURA trial support consolidation osimertinib after CRT for EGFR-mutated disease, with a marked progression-free survival benefit (HR 0.16). Shared regional gaps include limited screening uptake, variable reimbursement for molecular testing and targeted therapies, and uneven access to multidisciplinary care. Collectively, the available evidence suggests that earlier biomarker testing, structured nodule management pathways, and broader access to perioperative and consolidation therapies can meaningfully improve outcomes in Asian populations. Strengthening MDT integration and harmonising diagnostic and therapeutic workflows across settings remain essential next steps.

items.title: Anti-tumor immunotherapy, radiotherapy, and chemotherapy multimodal combination strategies and interactions in unresectable, locally advanced lung cancer: Clinical practice, mechanism, and biomarker research
items.authors: Xu Y, Guan H, Wu Y, et al.
items.abstract: Immunotherapy has fundamentally transformed the management of lung cancer. For unresectable, locally advanced non-small cell lung cancer (LA-NSCLC) and limited-stage small-cell lung cancer (LS-SCLC), the current standard of care is platinum-based concurrent chemoradiotherapy (cCRT) followed by consolidation immune-checkpoint blockade, a sequence that significantly prolongs progression-free and overall survival. Attempts to deliver immunotherapy concurrently with cCRT have not improved efficacy in randomized trials and have raised additional safety concerns. Induction chemotherapy plus immunotherapy followed by cCRT is biologically rational and feasible, but definitive benefit awaits phase III confirmation. Optimal sequencing, the most effective immunotherapeutic agents, and the best radiotherapy schedules remain active research priorities. The biological rationale for combining radiotherapy and chemotherapy with immunotherapy rests on their capacity to increase tumor immunogenicity, such as by releasing neoantigens, enhancing major histocompatibility complex-I (MHC-I) expression, and promoting dendritic-cell activation, thereby amplifying subsequent T-cell-mediated cytotoxicity. Yet the same cytotoxic stimuli concurrently elicit lymphodepletion, expand regulatory T cells, and trigger pro- inflammatory cytokine cascades that can blunt antitumor immunity. Consequently, the net therapeutic benefit depends on meticulous optimization of sequencing, fractionation, and dosing to harness immunostimulatory efects while minimizing immunosuppressive sequelae. Circulating tumor DNA, metabolic imaging parameters, and real-time immune-profiling are being integrated into non-invasive biomarker platforms that track response and guide post-concurrent chemoradiotherapy (cCRT) immunotherapy decisions. The next generation of curative-intent therapy will be defined by multidisciplinary, patient-centred treatment plans that combine advanced radiotherapy techniques to reduce toxicity, novel agents such as bispecific antibodies or antibody-drug conjugates, biomarker-driven precision medicine, and proactive adverse-event management.

items.title: MRI-guided HDR brachytherapy or integrated VMAT boost for tumour-targeted dose escalation in localised prostate cancer: long-term results of the TARGET study
items.authors: Padayachee J, Sanmamed NS, Ye XY, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: To evaluate local control of the gross tumour volume in localised prostate cancer following focal dose escalation delivered by integrated boost volumetric modulated arc therapy (IB-VMAT) or high-dose-rate (HDR) brachytherapy. Materials And Methods: Patients with localised prostate cancer and an intraprostatic lesion identified on multiparametric magnetic resonance imaging (mpMRI) were included in a prospective, non-randomised phase II study. Eighty patients received VMAT to the prostate 76 Gy/38 fractions. Boost strategy involved an IB of 95 Gy/38 fractions (IB-VMAT) or a single fraction of 10 Gy (HDR-VMAT). Three patients received 6 months androgen deprivation therapy. The primary endpoint was 3-year local control (LC) assessed by MRI or MRI-guided biopsy. Secondary outcomes included biochemical failure-free survival (bFFS), toxicity and health-related quality of life (HRQoL), assessed using CTCAE v.4.0, the American Urological Association Symptom Score and EPIC. Results: Median follow-up was 4.8 years (IQR, 4.0-8.0). Sixty-six patients underwent a 3-year MRI or MRI-guided biopsy; one patient demonstrated recurrence within the boost volume. Four patients demonstrated intraprostatic failure outside the boost volume and three patients developed regional/distant metastases. Eight patients experienced biochemical failure (4 IB-VMAT; 4 HDR-VMAT). Overall, 5-year bFFS was 86.9% (95% CI, 79.1-95.5). No substantial differences in late toxicities and HRQoL were observed between cohorts. Conclusion: Intraprostatic tumour-targeted dose escalation using IB-VMAT or HDR-VMAT provided high rates of LC and bFFS with limited adverse impact in late toxicity and HRQoL. Randomised studies are needed to further define the merits and differences between the two techniques.

items.title: Primary Endocrine Therapy vs Upfront Surgery for Older Women With Estrogen Receptor-Positive Breast Cancer: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.authors: Carleton N, Zou J, Mu Y, et al.
items.abstract: Importance: As the population of older women with breast cancer grows, an increasing number are considered for primary endocrine therapy (pET), yet clinicians lack a framework for identifying which patients are appropriate candidates, resulting in reliance on chronologic age and life expectancy rather than tumor biology. Objective: To evaluate survival and variables associated with response duration for patients treated with pET. Data Sources: PubMed, MEDLINE, Web of Science, and Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials were searched from inception through March 26, 2026. Study Selection: Randomized clinical trials (RCTs) and non-RCT (observational) cohorts comparing pET with surgery in operable, nonmetastatic, estrogen receptor (ER)-positive breast cancer. Data Extraction And Synthesis: Data were extracted independently by 2 reviewers per Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines. Hazard ratios (HRs) not directly reported were reconstructed from Kaplan-Meier curves. Randomized clinical trial-derived HRs for overall survival (OS) and breast cancer-specific survival (BCSS) were pooled using a random-effects model, given anticipated heterogeneity across trials spanning 5 decades and differing tumor biology criteria. Observational cohorts were analyzed descriptively, not pooled for comparative survival, given susceptibility to confounding by indication. Main Outcomes And Measures: The main outcomes were OS and BCSS (RCTs) assessed using meta-analysis. Time to progression, salvage intervention rates, and variables associated with progression and mortality (observational cohorts) were assessed using descriptive analyses. Results: Twenty-nine studies (6 RCTs and 23 observational cohorts; 22 821 patients; overall median [IQR] age, 83.1 [77.0-85.0] years) met the inclusion criteria. Patients from RCTs were generally younger (median [IQR] age, 77.0 [75.8-78.0] years) than those from the observational studies (median [IQR] age, 84.0 [81.5-86.0] years). Treatment with pET was not associated with a statistically significant OS difference vs surgery (HR, 1.14; 95% CI, 0.98-1.33), though the point estimate favored surgery. Median time to progression ranged from 19.7 months (range, 13.5-26.0 months) in tumor biology-unselected, tamoxifen-era cohorts to more than 50 months in ER-selected and aromatase inhibitor-treated cohorts. Tumor biology was consistently associated with progression risk.…

items.title: Pain Relief Without Financial Relief: Individual and Familial Financial Toxicity After Radiation Therapy for Spine Metastases in the Phase II SPORTSMEN Trial
items.authors: Stump A, Anwar M, Seekins C, et al.
items.abstract: Objectives: Prospective data on patient-reported financial toxicity (FT) during radiation therapy for spine metastases are limited. This secondary analysis of the SPORTSMEN trial (NCT05617716) characterized FT and quality of life, including changes 3 months after treatment. Methods: SPORTSMEN is a phase II trial randomizing patients with symptomatic spine metastases to SBRT (24 Gy/2 fractions or 19 Gy/1 fraction) or conventional EBRT (8 Gy/1 fraction). FT was measured with the COST-FACIT (lower scores indicate greater FT) and graded 0 (none) to 3 (severe); item 12 assessed familial hardship. Quality of life was measured with the EQ-5D-5L (higher scores indicate worse function) and EQ Visual Analog Scale (VAS). Analyses used Spearman correlation and the exact Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Results: Of 18 enrolled patients since 2025, 15 completed baseline COST-FACIT and 17 completed EQ-5D-5L. Eight (53%) had grade 1 to 2 FT. All patients with FT reported familial financial hardship, which correlated with FT grade (ρ=0.67, P=0.007). Pain was the most impaired domain (mean: 3.9, 71% severe or extreme). Among 7 patients with 3-month data, pain decreased from 4.3 to 2.3 (P=0.0625), EQ VAS rose from 44 to 64 (P=0.34), and FT increased from 2/7 patients to 5/7 patients. Conclusions: More than half of patients had FT before radiation therapy, closely tied to familial hardship. Although pain and self-rated health improved after treatment, FT did not. Financial screening and support for patients and families should begin at diagnosis and continue after treatment.

items.title: Non-fluorouracil/cisplatin versus fluorouracil/cisplatin regimens in chemoradiation for esophageal cancer: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.authors: Chen M, Ran J, Ding F, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Definitive concurrent chemoradiation (CCRT) is the standard treatment for unresectable locally advanced esophageal cancer (EC), with 5-fluorouracil and cisplatin (FP) as the conventional concurrent chemotherapy backbone. However, the comparative efficacy and toxicity of non-FP regimens remain unclear. Therefore, this systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to compare the efficacy and toxicity of non-FP regimens versus the standard FP regimen in definitive CCRT for locally advanced unresectable EC. Methods: We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis following PRISMA guidelines. PubMed, EMBASE, and the Cochrane Library were searched up to July 2026 for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and retrospective studies comparing at least two CCRT regimens. Meta-analysis was performed for RCTs directly comparing FP versus non-FP regimens; other comparisons were summarized narratively. Risk of bias was assessed using Cochrane RoB 2.0 for RCTs and the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale for observational studies. Results: Thirteen studies (9 RCTs, 4 retrospective; N=2,041) were included. Meta-analysis of four RCTs (n=955) showed no significant overall survival (OS) difference between non-FP and FP regimens [hazard ratio (HR) =0.94, 95% confidence interval (CI): 0.78-1.13; I2=0%]. Objective response rates (ORRs) and progression-free survival (PFS) varied substantially across studies. Grade ≥3 hematological toxicity differed significantly between specific regimens in six studies. Notably, 10 of 13 studies exclusively enrolled squamous cell carcinoma patients, and radiotherapy techniques/doses varied widely [intensity-modulated radiotherapy (IMRT) in 6 studies, three-dimensional conformal radiotherapy (3D-CRT) in 7; total doses 50-70 Gy], which complicates the attribution of non-hematological toxicities to chemotherapy alone. Conclusions: Pooled RCT evidence does not demonstrate an OS benefit of non-FP over FP in definitive CCRT for locally advanced EC. Given the predominance of squamous cell carcinoma and the heterogeneity in radiotherapy delivery, our findings are most applicable to this histology. Toxicity profiles vary, suggesting that patient tolerability should be a key consideration in regimen selection.

items.title: Radiosensitising strategies in locally advanced head and neck cancer: a systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials (RADIANCE-NMA)
items.authors: Mp S, Dange P, Rao KN, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Radiosensitiser enhance radiotherapy efficacy in locally advanced head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC). Although cisplatin-based chemoradiotherapy is the standard-of-care, over two dozen radiosensitising strategies have been evaluated in randomised trials with no network meta-analysis comparing all drug classes. Methods: PubMed, Embase, Cochrane CENTRAL, and ClinicalTrials.gov were searched from inception to 26 June 2026 for Phase IIb-III randomised controlled trials evaluating concurrent radiosensitiser therapy in adults with locally advanced head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (nasopharyngeal carcinoma excluded). Studies lacking overall survival data and induction-only comparisons were excluded. The primary outcome was overall survival (OS). All treatment-effect estimates are reported as hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Data were independently extracted by two reviewers. Risk of bias in individual trials was assessed with the Cochrane Risk of Bias (RoB 2) tool and confidence in the network estimates using the Confidence in Network Meta-Analysis (CINeMA) framework. Random-effects network meta-analysis was done with frequentist (netmeta) and Bayesian (gemtc) frameworks. Between-study heterogeneity was quantified using the I2 statistic and τ2; publication bias and small-study effects were assessed using comparison-adjusted funnel plots and Egger's regression test. This study is registered with the Open Science Framework (https://osf.io/cygsh). Findings: A total of 44 trials (13,768 patients; 84% male) were included in the primary analysis, with 23 additional trials in sensitivity analyses (67 total; 19,527 patients). Risk of bias showed some concerns in 39 of 44 (89%) primary trials on the Cochrane RoB 2 tool. Four treatments showed significant overall survival (OS) benefit versus radiotherapy alone: cisplatin plus 5-fluorouracil (hazard ratio (HR) 0.35; 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.18-0.66), nimotuzumab plus weekly cisplatin (0.48; 0.29-0.81), weekly cisplatin (0.57; 0.44-0.74), and three-weekly cisplatin (0.79; 0.65-0.95). In the network estimate, weekly cisplatin was favoured over three-weekly (HR 0.73; 0.58-0.93); the underlying randomised trials were designed as non-inferiority comparisons. Between-study heterogeneity was moderate (I2 = 48.9%; τ2 = 0.036; Cochran Q = 37.15, df = 19, p = 0.008), with no detected inconsistency (design-by-treatment global test p = 0.88).…

items.title: From synthesis to clinic: a task-specific framework for CT images metal artifact reduction in cervical brachytherapy
items.authors: Lu Y, Wang L, Wang Y, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Severe metal artifacts in cervical brachytherapy CT scans obscure critical anatomical structures and applicator geometry. Existing metal artifact reduction (MAR) models are inadequate in addressing these complex artifacts, leading to uncertainties in organs at risk (OARs) delineation and dose optimization that may compromise treatment safety and precision. This study aims to develop and validate a task-specific, synthetic-to-clinical deep learning framework for MAR in cervical brachytherapy CT scans. Methods: The synthetic dataset consisted of 500 external beam radiotherapy CT scans with simulated applicator artifacts from March 2021-April 2025. An independent clinical validation cohort included 50 brachytherapy CT scans. A proposed task-specific framework was applied to baseline deep learning MAR models, including InDuDoNet+, OSCNet+, OSCNet, and ADN. The performances of these models were compared against standard linear interpolation (LI) method and uncorrected images. Performance was assessed using quantitative metrics (peak signal-to-noise ratio [PSNR] and structural similarity index measure [SSIM]) on synthetic data, and clinical metrics (artifact index, applicator reconstruction error, and geometric accuracy of OARs) on clinical data. Additionally, three experienced radiologists independently evaluated the image quality using a 5-point Likert scale. Results: For the synthetic dataset, the proposed task-specific models significantly outperformed baseline models, with improvements of 32.42% in SSIM and 35.67% in PSNR (P < .001). Among the evaluated models, the task-specific InDuDoNet+ demonstrated superior performance (SSIM, 0.97; PSNR, 36.66 dB). In the clinical validation of 50 patients, task-specific models achieved significantly higher expert ratings (4.5 vs. 3.5 for uncorrected images) and exhibited an approximately 50% reduction in artifact indices for the bladder and rectum. Besides, the task-specific InDuDoNet+ model reduced the applicator reconstruction error to 0.1 mm, improved geometric contouring accuracy (Hausdorff distances < 1.0 mm for both bladder and rectum), and shortened contouring time by 30% to 40%. Conclusions: This study developed a task-specific deep learning framework to reduce brachytherapy CT metal artifacts while preserving anatomical details. The superior performance of the task-specific InDuDoNet+ model in improving geometric accuracy and workflow efficiency indicates that integrating this technology into clinical practice could significantly enhance the precision of cervical cancer brachytherapy.…

items.title: Perioperative immune checkpoint inhibition in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma: a 10-year review
items.authors: Freeman H, Rawson C, Al-Saidi N, et al.
items.abstract: Immune checkpoint blockade has transformed management of recurrent or metastatic head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC), yet efforts to integrate immunotherapy into curative chemoradiation have failed to improve outcomes. We conducted a narrative review of English-language literature published between 2015 and 2025, searching PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science, and ClinicalTrials.gov for perioperative (neoadjuvant and/or adjuvant) immunotherapy studies in resectable HNSCC, and reviewed translational and cross-tumor neoadjuvant data relevant to perioperative trial design. Across early-phase and randomized perioperative trials, neoadjuvant programmed cell death 1 (PD-1)-based strategies were consistently feasible and induced pathologic tumor regression in a subset of patients. Protocol-defined, treatment-related surgical delays were uncommon; however, delays overall were more frequent with perioperative pembrolizumab in the phase III setting (38 vs. 10 participants in KEYNOTE-689; median time to surgery 3.0 vs. 1.9 weeks), so preserved surgical deliverability should not be equated with absence of scheduling impact. Phase II studies associated depth of pathologic response and immune-inflamed tumor features with improved disease-free outcomes. These findings informed phase III perioperative trials, culminating in KEYNOTE-689, which improved event-free survival without compromising surgical completion. In contrast, phase III trials evaluating concurrent PD-1/programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) checkpoint blockade with definitive chemoradiotherapy showed no meaningful survival benefit. Collectively, current evidence supports perioperative pembrolizumab added to surgery and risk-adapted adjuvant therapy in selected patients with resectable locally advanced HNSCC, while other perioperative immune checkpoint inhibitor regimens remain investigational. This conclusion rests principally on a single positive phase III trial (KEYNOTE-689), and the June 2025 FDA approval is restricted to tumors with a PD-L1 combined positive score (CPS) of at least 1. The relative contributions of neoadjuvant priming, concurrent postoperative therapy, and prolonged adjuvant maintenance cannot be disentangled within the KEYNOTE-689 design, and no perioperative schedule can yet be designated optimal. Ongoing studies will refine biomarker-guided selection, sequencing, and duration.

items.title: Incidence of adverse events of concomitant immune checkpoint inhibitors and ultra hypo-fractionated radiotherapy: systematic review and meta-analysis
items.authors: Spindler NJ, Eefsen RL, Persson GF, et al.
items.abstract: Background: The combination of ultra hypofractionated radiotherapy (U-HFRT) and immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) has been proposed to increase systemic anti-tumor response, but the incidence of toxicity after concomitant ICI and U-HFRT remains to be explored. Methods: We performed a systematic review and meta-analysis of the incidence of adverse events (AEs) after concomitant ICI and U-HFRT in prospective trials, to evaluate whether ICI and U-HFRT were more toxic than ICI monotherapy. Eligible studies reported ≥10 adults treated with concomitant ICI and U-HFRT given to boost the immune response, here defined as ≥5 Gray per fraction and ≤ 10 fractions in total. The primary outcome was the incidence of selected National Cancer Institute Common Toxicity Criteria of Adverse Events (CTCAE) of any grade and grade 3-4 (G3-4). Secondary outcomes were median overall survival (mOS) and median progression-free survival (mPFS). The incidence of the AEs was calculated by a random-effects meta-analysis model and stratified by ICI drug groups, single vs. multiple fractions, and mean biological effective dose ≥44 Gy vs. < 44 Gy (mean BED). Quality assessment was performed with the McMaster Quality Assessment Scale for Harms (McHarm). Results: The meta-analysis included 2057 patients from 52 phase I-II and one phase III study. Overall, the most frequent G3-4 AEs were colitis (1.1%), pneumonitis (0.5%), and skin rash (0.2%). The incidence of any-grade pneumonitis was 3.3% in patients treated with anti-PD-1/PD-L1 and U-HFRT. The mOS and mPFS were 10.2 and 3.9 months across all cancer types, respectively. Conclusion: There was no consistent signal of increased incidence of systemic toxicity after concomitant U-HFRT and ICI in the phase I-III trials compared to previously reported toxicities of ICI monotherapy.

items.title: State-of-the-art treatment of Oesophagogastric junction adenocarcinoma: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials
items.authors: Rodríguez JV, Bonet M, Diez M, et al.
items.abstract: Oesophagogastric junction adenocarcinoma (OGJ AC) represents an increasingly prevalent malignancy for which treatment recommendations remain challenging, as patients are frequently included within trials addressing gastric or oesophageal cancer. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials (RCTs) published between 2000 and 2025 including patients with OGJ AC to provide a comprehensive assessment of contemporary treatment strategies for this disease across all stages. A total of 100 high-quality RCTs including more than 13,000 patients with OGJ tumours were identified. In localized disease, 36 studies evaluated surgical procedures, adjuvant/neoadjuvant/perioperative treatments and definitive approaches. Surgery is still the cornerstone of curative treatment, increasingly incorporating minimally invasive techniques. Perioperative chemotherapy and chemoimmunotherapy represent standard approaches, while neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy followed by adjuvant nivolumab represents an alternative strategy. In advanced disease, 64 studies assessed systemic therapies in first/second/third lines or palliative interventions. Platinum-fluoropyrimidine chemotherapy persists as the backbone of first-line treatment, with treatment intensification guided by biomarkers. While the benefit of trastuzumab in HER2-positive tumours appears greater in OGJ than in gastric cancer, the opposite pattern is observed with zolbetuximab in CLDN18.2-positive tumours. Several trials testing anti-PD-1 therapies confirm their activity in OGJ AC, despite the predictive value of PD-L1 appearing uncertain in this anatomical subgroup. In later lines, paclitaxel plus ramucirumab, trastuzumab deruxtecan for HER2-positive disease, and trifluridine-tipiracil remain established options. The available evidence suggests clinically meaningful differences in treatment efficacy according to tumour location, supporting the consideration of OGJ AC as a distinct disease entity. Dedicated OGJ AC trials incorporating standardized anatomical classification are needed to improve outcomes in this aggressive disease.

items.title: Immunochemotherapy for Borderline Resectable or Locally Advanced Pancreatic Cancer: A Randomized Controlled Trial
items.authors: Bai X, Li X, Chen Y, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: The optimal treatment strategy for patients with borderline resectable pancreatic cancer (BRPC) and locally advanced pancreatic cancer (LAPC) remains undefined. We evaluated whether the addition of programmed cell death protein 1 blockade to modified FOLFIRINOX improves outcomes compared with modified FOLFIRINOX alone. Methods: In this open-label, randomized phase II trial, patients with histologically confirmed BRPC or LAPC were randomly assigned (1:1) to receive modified FOLFIRINOX plus toripalimab (immunochemotherapy) or modified FOLFIRINOX alone (chemotherapy). Treatment response was assessed every 2 months, and surgical eligibility was determined by a multidisciplinary team. The primary end point was event-free survival (EFS) in the intention-to-treat population. Results: Between April 2019 and March 2025, 392 patients were randomly assigned to immunochemotherapy (n = 196) or chemotherapy (n = 196). After a median follow-up of 39.6 months, immunochemotherapy significantly improved EFS compared with chemotherapy (median, 11.1 v 9.6 months; hazard ratio [HR], 0.74 [95% CI, 0.60 to 0.92]; P = .007). The median overall survival (OS) was 20.6 versus 17.1 months (HR, 0.81; 95% CI, 0.63 to 1.03). Objective response rates were 30.1% (59/196) and 18.9% (37/196), respectively. Tumor resection rates were 42.3% (83/196) and 43.9% (86/196), and R0 resection rates were 84.1% (69/82) and 74.7% (62/83), respectively. Prespecified subgroup analyses suggested improved EFS and OS in BRPC but not LAPC. Grade 3 or higher adverse events occurred in 47.9% (93/194) and 49.2% (96/195) of patients receiving immunochemotherapy and chemotherapy, respectively. Grade III or higher postoperative complications occurred in 30.1% (25/83) and 25.6% (22/86) of resected patients. Conclusion: The addition of PD-1 blockade to modified FOLFIRINOX significantly improved EFS without increasing treatment-related toxicity or surgical morbidity in patients with BRPC or LAPC.

items.title: Stereotactic Ablative Radiotherapy Versus Surgical Resection for Early-Stage Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer: An Emulated Target Trial
items.authors: Kagenaar E, Lugo-Palacios DG, Aggarwal A, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: Stereotactic ablative radiotherapy (SABR) is standard of care for inoperable early-stage non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), but there is little evidence to support SABR as an alternative to surgical resection. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) have failed to recruit, and ongoing RCTs apply strict inclusion criteria. To our knowledge, this is the first emulated target trial comparing the effectiveness of SABR versus surgery in individuals with early-stage NSCLC eligible for either treatment. Methods: We used England's National Cancer Registry data to identify individuals diagnosed with T1-2N0M0 NSCLC during 2015-2020, age 18-79 years with Zubrod performance status 0-2, or age 80+ years with performance status 0-1, who underwent SABR or surgical resection within 6 months of diagnosis. Treatment receipt was identified via linkage to Hospital Episode Statistics and the National Radiotherapy Data Set. The primary outcome was 3-year all-cause mortality; secondary outcomes included lung cancer-specific mortality and recurrence. An instrumental variable analysis reduced the risk of confounding by indication. Results: A total of 12,546 met the eligibility criteria (2,299 SABR; 10,247 surgery). After adjustment, 3-year all-cause mortality estimates were 30.3% (SABR) and 21.6% (surgery; mean absolute risk difference 8.8 percentage points [pp], [95% CI, 1.4 to 16.2]; P = .02). Lung cancer-specific mortality estimates were 20.6% (SABR) and 14.5% (surgery; mean absolute risk difference 6.1 pp [95% CI, -0.6 to 12.9]; P = .07). The adjusted mean absolute risk difference in 3-year all-cause mortality for those age 80+ years was 4.3 pp ([95% CI, -3.7 to 12.3]; P = .62). Conclusion: This emulated target trial found higher 3-year all-cause mortality after SABR versus surgery in early-stage NSCLC suitable for either modality, supporting that surgical resection should remain the preferred option. The findings support SABR as a curative-intent alternative, particularly for older people.

items.title: Expansion of the Inpatient Metastatic Spine Score to Outpatients With Spine Metastases: Prospective Assessment on an Ongoing Phase 2 Randomized Controlled Trial
items.authors: McClelland S 3rd
items.abstract: Objectives: For inpatients with spinal metastases, the Inpatient Metastatic Spine Score accurately assesses prognosis, with scores of 0 to 3 exhibiting significantly longer survival than scores >3. This study examines the accuracy of this algorithm for outpatients prospectively considered for enrollment in the Spine Patient Optimal Radiosurgery Treatment for Symptomatic MEtastatic Neoplasms (SPORTSMEN) phase II randomized controlled trial. Methods: From July 2025 to January 2026, outpatients at an NCI-designated cancer center were evaluated. Prognosis was assessed per an adjusted Metastatic Spine Score adjusted for consisting of: age at presentation (60+ vs. younger), duration of metastatic disease diagnosis (6+ mo vs. sooner), refractory to or on active systemic therapy (yes/no), additional nonspine metastatic focus (yes/no), severe malnutrition of chronic disease (yes/no), brain metastases (yes/no), and presenting symptomatology (asymptomatic or spine/back pain alone=no; additional neurological symptoms=yes) with each category scored a 0 (no) or 1 (yes) and a cumulative score derived. Scores of 0 to 3 were compared with scores >3 and correlated with outcomes. Positive prognosis=time to death/hospice >90 days from presentation. The Fisher test was used for statistical analysis. Results: A positive prognosis was exhibited in 8/9 patients with scores of 0 to 3 (8/8 patients without brain metastases) versus 3/9 patients with scores >3 (P=0.0498). The overall accuracy of the Metastatic Spine Score (8/9 positive + 6/9 negative=14/18 patients) was 78%. Conclusion: The Metastatic Spine Score provides an accurate prognostic assessment of outpatients with spine metastases, with scores of 0 to 3 yielding significantly better prognosis than scores >3. These findings also support brain MRI evaluation before radiotherapy decisions regarding spinal metastases. This study adds further support for establishing the Metastatic Spine Score as the standard-of-care for accurately evaluating prognosis in this patient population for outpatients as well as inpatients.

items.title: Spine Patient Optimal Radiosurgery Treatment for Symptomatic Metastatic Neoplasms (SPORTSMEN): Time to Treatment Outcomes From a Multicenter Phase II Randomized Controlled Trial
items.authors: McClelland S 3rd, Onyewadume L, Anwar M
items.abstract: Objectives: For treatment of spine metastases, stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) has been proven to yield improved local control durability compared with external beam radiation therapy (EBRT) despite requiring more complexity in treatment planning. The time to initiation of treatment is an important consideration in this patient population, yet has rarely been assessed. We present our findings regarding this aspect of care from the Spine Patient Optimal Radiosurgery Treatment for Symptomatic MEtastatic Neoplasms (SPORTSMEN) phase II multicenter randomized controlled trial. Methods: In the SPORTSMEN trial, patients with symptomatic spine metastases are randomized to SBRT (24 Gy in 2 fractions, 19 Gy in 1 fraction) versus EBRT (8 Gy in 1 fraction). The primary trial endpoint is 3-month pain freedom, using the Brief Pain Inventory. The time from patient randomization to treatment initiation was assessed and compared between SBRT and EBRT. Results: Of the first 26 patients treated in the study, 19 received SBRT, and 7 received EBRT. The mean time from randomization to treatment (TRT) for EBRT was 3.7 days (SD±2.36) versus 10.3 days (SD±5.79) for SBRT. This difference in TRT of 6.6 days was statistically significant (P=0.0079). Conclusion: Level I evidence indicates that compared with EBRT, patients with symptomatic spine metastatic disease receiving SBRT experience an ∼1-week delay in starting treatment. This finding should play a role in informed consent discussions with patients, particularly those who are already symptomatic from their metastatic disease.

items.title: HB0025 With Chemotherapy for Advanced Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer: A Phase 2 Nonrandomized Clinical Trial
items.authors: Zhou F, Wang L, Bai J, et al.
items.abstract: Importance: Bispecific antibodies targeting vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) and programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1)/PD-1 ligand 1 (PD-L1) pathways represent a promising therapeutic strategy for advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). HB0025 is a novel bispecific antibody fusion targeting PD-L1 and VEGF. Objective: To evaluate the efficacy and safety of HB0025 plus chemotherapy in previously untreated advanced, driver variant-negative NSCLC. Design, Setting, And Participants: This open-label, multicenter, phase 2 nonrandomized clinical trial enrolled patients with stage IIIB/C or IV NSCLC without sensitizing EGFR, ALK, or ROS1 alterations across 13 hospitals in China. Participants included those with nonsquamous NSCLC and squamous NSCLC. Patients were enrolled from January 15, 2024, to May 21, 2025. Data cutoff was April 20, 2026. Interventions: Patients received intravenous 10-mg/kg HB0025 every 3 weeks or 20-mg/kg HB0025 every 3 weeks plus chemotherapy: pemetrexed/carboplatin for nonsquamous and paclitaxel/carboplatin for squamous for up to 6 cycles, followed by HB0025 maintenance (with pemetrexed for nonsquamous) until disease progression or unacceptable toxic effects. Main Outcomes And Measures: The primary end points were safety and investigator-assessed objective response rate (ORR) per Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors, version 1.1. The secondary end points included disease control rate, duration of response, progression-free survival (PFS), and overall survival (OS). Results: Treatment efficacy was evaluable in 169 enrolled patients. The nonsquamous cohort included 85 patients (median [IQR] age, 63.0 [58.0-68.0] years; 26 [30.6%] female and 59 [69.4%] male patients), and the squamous cohort included 84 patients (median [IQR] age, 65.0 [60.0-69.0] years; 6 [7.1%] female and 78 [92.9%] male patients). In the nonsquamous cohort, confirmed ORR was 36.4% (95% CI, 17.2%-59.3%) and 57.1% (95% CI, 44.1%-69.5%) in the 10-mg/kg and 20-mg/kg dose groups, respectively. In the squamous cohort, ORR reached 68.2% (95% CI, 45.1%-86.1%) and 74.2% (95%, 61.5%-84.5%) at the respective doses. Median PFS was 12.52 months (95% CI, 10.15-16.56) in the nonsquamous cohort and 14.78 months (95% CI, 11.30 to not estimable) in the squamous cohort. The 12-month PFS rates were 54.3% (95% CI, 41.6%-65.3%) and 62.1% (95% CI, 49.9%-72.1%) in the nonsquamous and squamous cohorts, and the 12-month OS rates were 75.8% (95% CI, 65.0%-83.7%) and 85.5% (95% CI, 75.8%-91.5%) , respectively.…

items.title: Image-Based Consensus Molecular Subtyping Refines Prognostication in Stage II/III Colorectal Cancer: A Retrospective Analysis of the SCOT Trial
items.authors: Lafarge MW, Harkin A, Iveson T, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: Risk stratification in localized colorectal cancer (CRC) remains inadequate. Transcriptome-based classifiers such as consensus molecular subtyping (CMS) improve this, but are challenging to implement. We determined the performance of a novel image-based method for CRC CMS subtyping (imCMS) using routine pathology images from the SCOT trial and investigated association of imCMS subtypes with clinicopathologic and tumor molecular and immune factors, treatment benefit, and survival. Methods: We applied a novel imCMS classifier to stage II/III CRCs from the SCOT trial (ISRCTN59757862) which examined 3 versus 6 months of adjuvant oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy following curative-intent surgery. We determined correlates of imCMS subgroups and investigated imCMS prognostic and predictive value for CRC recurrence-free interval, overall survival (OS), and survival after CRC recurrence (SAR) by univariable and multivariable Cox regression. Results: A total of 2,816 cases were informative for imCMS classification, of which 664 (24%) were imCMS1 (immune), 987 (35%) imCMS2 (canonical), 433 (15%) imCMS3 (metabolic), 653 (23%) imCMS4 (mesenchymal), and 79 (3%) of mixed subtype. Analysis confirmed expected associations of imCMS1 with deficient DNA mismatch repair (dMMR) and imCMS3 with KRAS mutation and revealed substantially lower intraepithelial CD8+ and intrastromal FoxP3+ T-cell infiltrate (CD8IE-FoxP3IS) in imCMS4 tumors. imCMS classification was strongly prognostic independent of clinicopathologic factors, dMMR, and CD8IE-FoxP3IS in multivariable analysis but did not predict differential benefit from chemotherapy duration or regimen. The combination of imCMS with CD8IE-FoxP3IS groups defined CRC subgroups with substantially different recurrence risk. Analysis of OS and SAR revealed notable discordance in imCMS3 and imCMS4 prognostic value before and after relapse. Conclusion: imCMS classification improves CRC prognostication beyond existing tumor factors and is potentially deliverable in clinical practice. imCMS prediction of therapeutic benefit requires further study.

items.title: Preliminary Dose Constraints for Testing Intensity Modulated Proton Therapy in Anal Cancer Trials
items.authors: Krishnatry R, Jain A, Punde R, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: The target volume for radiotherapy of anal cancer is complex, with the added challenge of it being surrounded by several critical organs at risk (OARs). In this study, we review the dosimetric advantage that can be achieved with intensity modulated proton therapy (IMPT) over intensity modulated radiotherapy (IMRT) and derive the dose constraints for OARs. Materials And Methods: Ten consecutive patients of anal cancer treated using rotational IMRT (Rapid Arc; Varian Medical Systems, Palo Alto, USA) in 2023 were reviewed. The contours of the target volumes and OARs (bowel, bladder, marrow, bilateral femoral heads, and external genitalia) were reviewed on Eclipse (v16.1) treatment planning system for adherence to contouring guidelines. The clinical plans were re-evaluated for OAR doses and target volume coverage.The scans with structure sets were exported to RayStation treatment planning system (v12A) for intensity modulated proton therapy (IMPT) planning. The dose for IMPT planning was prescribed to the CTV with 5 mm robustness, keeping dose prescription similar to the clinical IMRT plan (45-50 Gy to pelvis and 55-60 Gy simultaneous boost to any gross disease and gross nodes). The 4 beam class solution was identified as best for IMPT planning. The IMPT plan objective was set 10% to 20% below the lower threshold of RTOG 05-29 and UK guidelines, followed by principles of ALARA for OARs without compromising target coverage. The dose-volume parameters, conformity index (CI) and homogeneity index (HI) were compared for IMRT versus IMPT using student's t-test. Results: Target volume coverage was well achieved with both IMRT and IMPT. However, V100% of GTVp and GTVn and V95%, V98%, V99%, V100% of CTVPelvis and CTVTumourBoost were significantly better with IMPT. HI and CI of target volumes were also significantly improved with IMPT. There was a significant decrease in volume of OARs receiving doses <40 Gy. Volumes receiving higher doses (40-50 Gy) were very small and not significantly affected with use of IMPT. Conclusion: IMPT offers improved target coverage with reduction in low-intermediate dose spill to OARs. Based on these results, dose constraints for IMPT planning have been generated for future clinical trial validation.

items.title: Regulatable membrane-bound IL-15 engineered TIL cell therapy for immune checkpoint inhibitor-resistant advanced melanoma: pooled analysis of phase 1 and 1/2 trials
items.authors: Amaria RN, Chesney JA, Betof AS, et al.
items.abstract: Amsokigene autoleucel (amsoki-cel, OBX-115) is a tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte (TIL) cell therapy engineered to express acetazolamide (ACZ)-regulatable membrane-bound interleukin-15, abrogating the need for interleukin-2. In two single-arm trials (completed phase 1 single-center first-in-human (FIH) and ongoing phase 1/2 multicenter Agni-01), patients with immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI)-resistant advanced melanoma received lymphodepletion and varying doses and schedules of amsoki-cel and ACZ. The primary objective of FIH and Agni-01 phase 1 was safety, tolerability and recommended phase 2 dose (RP2D); the primary objective of Agni-01 phase 2 was objective response rate (ORR) at the RP2D. The first patient treated experienced rapid lymphocyte expansion and vasogenic edema of a previously irradiated brain metastasis, prompting protocol modifications and dose deescalation in FIH, including 80% reduction in maximum amsoki-cel dose and 75% reduction in ACZ dose. After preliminary demonstration of safety at the lower dose, doses were increased in FIH, and reescalation was initiated in Agni-01. Across studies, 37 patients were treated (FIH, n = 17; Agni-01, n = 20). Post hoc pooled analysis demonstrated no dose-limiting toxicities, ICU care or treatment-related mortality. Most common grade 3 or higher treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) included neutropenia (64.9% (24/37)), leukopenia/lymphopenia (56.8% (21/37) each) and anemia/thrombocytopenia (37.8% (14/37) each). Serious TEAEs were reported for 10 patients, including eight patients with grade 3 or higher events (non-hematologic, 13.5% (5/37); hematologic, 13.5% (5/37)). RP2D was selected based on overall safety and tolerability as well as preliminary anti-tumor activity in Agni-01 phase 1. The phase 2 preliminary ORR was 66.7% (6/9). In total, 15 patients were treated at RP2D and comprise the Key Efficacy Set (Agni-01: phase 1, n = 6; phase 2, n = 9), of which 10 patients (66.7%; 95% confidence interval 38-88%) achieved objective responses (including two complete responses). Amsoki-cel demonstrated favorable safety and promising early clinical activity in patients with ICI-resistant melanoma. A separate phase 2 pivotal Agni-01 cohort is ongoing. ClinicalTrials.gov identifiers: NCT05470283 and NCT06060613 .

items.title: Low-dose radiotherapy for spinal facet joint osteoarthritis: a rational extension or a bridge too far?
items.authors: Hammadeh BM, Mohamad I, Abuhijla F
items.abstract: Purpose: This work critically evaluates whether the existing evidence for low-dose radiotherapy (LDRT) in peripheral osteoarthritis can be extrapolated to lumbar facet joint osteoarthritis. Moreover, it aims to determine whether current data justify its routine clinical use or only further investigation in this specific spinal indication. Methods: This commentary study synthesizes preclinical data on the anti-inflammatory effects of low-dose irradiation, observational studies reporting symptomatic relief in appendicular osteoarthritis, and higher-level evidence from randomized sham-controlled trials and meta-analyses. It also compares anatomical and biological risks unique to the lumbar spine, particularly vertebral bone marrow exposure and hematologic malignancy potential, and assesses whether modern radiation techniques (e.g., volumetric modulated arc therapy) sufficiently mitigate these risks. Results: Preclinical and observational data suggest anti-inflammatory activity and possible symptomatic improvement with LDRT, but randomized sham-controlled trials and recent meta-analyses fail to confirm significant clinical benefit. The lumbar spine poses additional safety concerns due to its proximity to active bone marrow, and while advanced delivery methods reduce marrow exposure, they do not eliminate it. No spine-specific efficacy or long-term safety data currently exist. Conclusion: Current evidence is insufficient to support routine clinical implementation of LDRT for lumbar facet joint osteoarthritis. The treatment should remain investigational, with a structured research agenda including dosimetric studies, prospective feasibility cohorts, registry surveillance, and long-term sham-controlled trials, which are required to establish both efficacy and safety before any clinical adoption.

items.title: HB0025, a Novel Anti–PD-L1/VEGF Trap Bispecific Antibody Plus Chemotherapy in Advanced NSCLC
items.abstract: The article by Zhou et al evaluates the efficacy and safety of HB0025, a novel programmed cell death 1 ligand 1 (PD-L1) and vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) trap bispecific antibody plus chemotherapy in patients with advanced treatment–naive, EGFR/ALK/ROS1–negative non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) across multiple Chinese sites demonstrating impressive antitumor efficacy with a manageable safety profile. Results from this trial add to a growing body of evidence for combined programmed cell death 1 protein (PD-1)/PD-L1 and VEGF pathway inhibition in NSCLC—an approach being investigated with multiple bispecific agents across both phase 2 and phase 3 trials. How to optimize patient selection for such agents among a global population remains a key question.

items.title: Treatment-Response Evidence, Care-Pathway Gaps, and Guideline Discordance in Gastric MALT Lymphoma: An Umbrella Review
items.authors: Gong EJ, Bang CS, Baik GH, et al.
items.abstract: Background/Aims: Reviews of gastric mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue lymphoma have quantified treatment response, but their coverage of the care pathway and relationship to guideline differences remain unclear. Methods: PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were searched through March 31, 2026. Eligible reviews were mapped to 13 clinical questions as direct, partial, or absent coverage. Question-specific anchors were selected without pooling overlapping reviews. All 16 items of A MeaSurement Tool to Assess systematic Reviews, version 2 were examined; overall confidence was assigned to intervention reviews. European Gastro-Intestinal Lymphoma Study, European Society for Medical Oncology, National Comprehensive Cancer Network, and British Society for Haematology recommendations were compared descriptively. Results: Fifteen reviews were eligible; nine reviews answered seven questions. Complete remission was 75.2% after successful Helicobacter pylori eradication in H. pylori-positive disease. In H. pylori-negative disease, source-defined complete remission was 29.3%, including probable minimal residual disease. Remission was 22.2% in patients with t(11;18)/BIRC3::MALT1-positive disease versus 78.0% in patients with translocation-negative disease. The radiotherapy remission estimates were 97.3% after eradication failure and 96.0% in the limited-stage cohort. Gastric positron emission tomography (PET) detection was 62.0%, without evidence of management benefit. All eight intervention reviews had critically low confidence; seven nonintervention reviews received descriptive profiles. The guidelines differed for H. pylori-negative management, endoscopic ultrasonography, bone marrow biopsy, and PET/computed tomography. No eligible review compared the relevant treatment sequences or staging strategies. Conclusions: Review-level evidence is concentrated on treatment response. It cannot establish superiority between treatment sequences or determine staging, escalation timing, surveillance, or relapse strategies. Guideline differences concern decisions for which the relevant comparisons remain unsynthesized.

items.title: [Comment] Mastering the role of radiotherapy in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma: who and why?
items.authors: Guler Yavas, Rohan K Patel, Christina Small-Tom, Beth Erickson, William A Hall
items.abstract: For the past decade, radiotherapy in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) has been evaluated in randomised trials1–5 with mixed results. Over that same period, radiotherapy delivery techniques have improved substantially.6 Radiotherapy today is materially better than it was 10 years ago. It is more accurate and normal organ dose constraints are better understood. Radiation oncologists comprehend the modality better, especially stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT). Categorically, SBRT is still evolving for PDAC and we are still evaluating the optimal way in which SBRT should be given.

items.title: Amrecibart and cenvacibart for the prevention of catheter-related thrombosis (ROXI-CATH): a double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled, phase 2 trial
items.authors: Zwicker JI, Kithcart AP, Kaplan J, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Peripherally inserted central catheters (PICCs) are often complicated by venous thromboembolism, yet no thromboprophylaxis is approved. Factor XI (FXI) inhibition might prevent catheter-associated venous thromboembolism without increasing bleeding. We evaluated the safety and efficacy of amrecibart and cenvacibart for preventing venous thromboembolism after PICC placement. Methods: ROXI-CATH is a double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled, phase 2 trial conducted across 12 hospital centres in Bulgaria, Canada, Israel, Romania, the UK, and the USA. Eligible participants aged 18 years or older undergoing PICC insertion, with the PICC expected to remain for at least 14 days, and an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status of 2 or less were randomly assigned (1:1:1) using a permuted block design and stratified by site and diagnosis of active cancer to receive a single intravenous infusion of amrecibart (300 mg; anti-FXI A2 domain monoclonal antibody), cenvacibart (250 mg; anti-FXI catalytic domain monoclonal antibody), or placebo. Participants, principal investigators, and study site staff were masked to treatment assignment. The primary efficacy outcome was adjudicated venous thromboembolism (symptomatic or asymptomatic PICC-associated deep vein thrombosis or superficial vein thrombosis, or pulmonary embolism, including pulmonary embolism-related death) up to day 14. Ultrasounds were performed on days 7 and 14. The key secondary efficacy outcome was adjudicated thrombosis detected by ultrasound in the upper extremity with the PICC up to day 14. The primary safety outcome was site-reported treatment-emergent adverse events up to the end of the study. The key secondary safety outcomes were adjudicated major and clinically relevant non-major (CRNM) bleeding up to day 14. Efficacy analyses were performed in the full analysis set, which consisted of all randomly assigned participants who received any study drug and with any evaluable post-baseline ultrasound or a confirmed episode of venous thromboembolism. Safety analyses were performed in the safety analysis set, which included all randomly assigned participants who received any study drug (as treated). This trial is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT06299111 (completed; these analyses were performed after database lock on May 6, 2026). Findings: Between Sept 20, 2024, and Dec 19, 2025, 240 participants were screened, and 195 were randomly assigned to amrecibart (n=65), cenvacibart (n=66), or placebo (n=64).…

items.title: Neurocognitive function and quality of life results from a phase II study (NRG/RTOG 0424) of temozolomide-based chemoradiotherapy regimen for high-risk low-grade gliomas
items.journal: Int J Radiat Oncol Biol Phys
items.authors: Wefel JS, Pugh SL, Choucair AK, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: This analysis of NRG/RTOG 0424 describes post-treatment changes in neurocognitive function (NCF) and quality of life (QOL) in patients with high-risk low-grade glioma (HR-LGG). Methods: Patients with HR-LGG were treated with radiation and concurrent and adjuvant temozolomide (RT-TMZ). Standardized NCF tests were performed at baseline, 6, and 12 months. Rates of change in NCF were examined using the reliable change index (RCI) on Hopkins Verbal Learning Test (HVLT), Trail Making Test (TMT), and Controlled Oral Word Association (COWA). Relationships between NCF and subjective cognitive concerns (MOS-CF) were evaluated. QOL was assessed using Functional Assessment of Cancer Therapy - Brain (FACT-Br). Longitudinal modeling evaluated predictors of change in NCF and QOL. Cox models assessed the association of baseline NCF with overall survival (OS). Results: From January 2005 to August 2009, 129 evaluable patients were accrued, and 93 completed at least the baseline and one post-treatment NCF/QOL measurement. RCI-determined decline occurred in 50% and 40% at 6 and 12 months, respectively and was most frequent on HVLT (21%, 20%), TMTA (29%, 20%), and TMTB (22%, 14%). MID-determined QOL decline on the FACT-Brain Subscale occurred in about 25% at 6 and 12 months. Several tumor and clinical characteristics were associated with worse NCF including tumor crossing the midline, the number of high-risk factors, and EORTC OS risk group. Conclusions: Many patients with HR-LGG experience NCF decline in the first year after treatment with temozolomide-based concurrent chemoradiation. QOL remained stable or improved. Ongoing studies with integrated NCF monitoring using these tests will aid clinicians and patients in treatment decisions that seek to consider oncologic and functional outcomes.

items.title: Efficacy and safety of stereotactic body radiotherapy combined with immune checkpoint inhibitors for non-small cell lung cancer: a systematic review and reconstructed individual patient data meta-analysis
items.authors: Ji P, Zhao Z, Tang X, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) may augment antitumor immunity when combined with immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), but clinical studies span markedly different disease stages and treatment intents and have produced inconsistent comparative results. We aimed to synthesize the evidence and evaluate efficacy and safety, separating pairwise outcomes from descriptive single-arm outcomes. Methods: PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), and ClinicalTrials.gov were searched from inception through August 2026. Pairwise outcomes were synthesized as risk ratios (RRs) or reconstructed survival hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence interval (CI). Single-arm outcomes of SBRT plus ICI were summarized as pooled proportions. Published Kaplan-Meier curves were digitized and reconstructed as individual patient data (IPD). Disease-stage and treatment-setting analyses were prespecified as descriptive because they were based on unadjusted between-study comparisons. Results: Twenty-one studies enrolling 1,096 participants were included. Five comparative studies contributed to at least one pairwise outcome. SBRT plus ICI was not associated with statistically significant improvements in overall survival (OS) (HR 0.81, 95% CI: 0.52-1.25), progression-free survival (PFS) (HR 0.76, 95% CI: 0.53-1.10), or objective response rate (ORR) (RR 1.72, 95% CI: 0.85-3.51). Disease control rate (DCR) favored SBRT plus ICI (RR 1.20, 95% CI: 1.03-1.39), but significance was lost when either of two influential studies was omitted. Pairwise risks of any-grade and grade ≥3 adverse events (AEs) did not differ significantly. In descriptive single-arm analyses, median OS was 36.4 months (95% CI: 29.8-50.9) and median PFS was 14.6 months (95% CI: 11.6-17.2); pooled ORR was 49.4% (95% CI: 38.0-60.8%), DCR was 80.6% (95% CI: 70.9-87.7%), any-grade AE incidence was 74.2% (95% CI: 50.3-89.1%), and grade ≥3 AE incidence was 27.1% (95% CI: 17.1-40.2%). Conclusions: The comparative pairwise meta-analysis does not demonstrate an OS, PFS, or ORR benefit from adding SBRT to ICI-based treatment. Although the primary DCR estimate was statistically significant, its sensitivity to individual studies and the low certainty of evidence preclude a firm efficacy conclusion. Setting-specific randomized trials with standardized radiation, outcome, and toxicity definitions are needed.

items.title: The Impact of Narrative Nursing on Psychological Distress, Coping Styles, and Quality of Life in Patients With Cancer Undergoing Radiation Therapy
items.authors: Feng Q, Wu H, Liu N, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: To investigate the effect of a narrative nursing intervention on psychological distress, coping styles, and quality of life and provide a basis for improving psychological health and overall well-being in patients with cancer undergoing outpatient radiation therapy. Participants And Setting: This randomized controlled trial enrolled 62 patients with malignant tumors who were receiving outpatient radiation therapy at Xiangya Hospital of Central South University in Changsha, China. Participants were recruited from April 2023 to May 2025. Methodologic Approach: Patients were randomly assigned to the usual care group (N = 31) or the narrative nursing intervention group (N = 31). Both groups received standard outpatient radiation therapy care, and the intervention group underwent an additional six-week narrative nursing intervention. Evaluations were performed using a general information questionnaire, the National Comprehensive Cancer Network distress management screening measure, the Medical Coping Modes Questionnaire, and the Functional Assessment of Cancer Therapy-General prior to the first radiation therapy session and within one week after the final session. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. Findings: A total of 62 patients were enrolled and completed the study. After the intervention, psychological distress scores were significantly lower in the narrative nursing intervention group compared to the usual care group (p < 0.05). Postintervention, significant differences were observed in all coping dimensions (confrontation, avoidance, and resignation) in the intervention group after adjusting for baseline characteristics (p < 0.05). The intervention group also exhibited significantly higher overall quality-of-life scores, as well as improvements in physical, social/family, emotional, and functional well-being, compared to the usual care group (p < 0.05). Implications For Nursing: A narrative nursing intervention can effectively alleviate psychological distress, optimize coping strategies, and enhance quality of life for patients undergoing radiation therapy in the outpatient setting.

items.title: Lessons learned from a decade of EUS(-FNA) staging in esophageal and GEJ carcinoma: towards a selective staging strategy
items.authors: Quik JSE, van Sandick JW, Owers EC, et al.
items.abstract: Endoscopic ultrasonography with fine-needle aspiration (EUS(-FNA)) is recommended by current guidelines as part of the staging for esophageal and gastro-esophageal junction (GEJ) carcinoma, yet its incremental value over modern 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (FDG-PET) remains uncertain. This Lessons Learned article reflects on over a decade of EUS(-FNA) and FDG-PET staging in 402 patients with potentially curable esophageal or GEJ carcinoma at a high-volume tertiary referral center. In 91.3% of patients, EUS(-FNA) did not alter the radiation field as would have been defined by FDG-PET. EUS(-FNA) resulted in an expansion of the radiation field in 4.5% and reduction in 4.2% of patients. Squamous cell carcinoma showed more than two-fold greater likelihood of radiation field modification. Among 193 patients classified as FDG-PET non-suspicious for malignant lymph nodes (LNs), EUS-FNA identified malignant LNs in eight patients (4.1%), which influenced the radiation field. In 5 of 402 patients (1.2%) a malignant LN was detected with EUS-FNA in a station that would not have routinely been resected surgically. In patients planned for neoadjuvant or definitive chemoradiotherapy (CRT), LN staging is of direct therapeutic consequence: underestimation of nodal disease may result in geographic miss, while overestimation leads to unnecessary irradiation. In contrast, in patients treated with perioperative 5-fluorouracil, leucovorin, oxaliplatin and docetaxel (FLOT) followed by surgical lymphadenectomy, most involved LN stations are routinely addressed surgically, limiting the added value of EUS(-FNA) for treatment planning. Therefore, we view EUS(-FNA) as a selective staging tool in patients planned for neoadjuvant or definitive CRT, rather than a procedure applied routinely to all patients.

items.title: Neoadjuvant botensilimab with or without balstilimab in pMMR and dMMR colon cancer: the phase 2 UNICORN trial
items.authors: Ghelardi F, Ambrosini M, Raimondi A, et al.
items.abstract: Preoperative immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) are active in patients with deficient mismatch repair (dMMR) colon cancer (CC), whereas proficient mismatch repair (pMMR) CC has been consistently considered resistant to first-generation ICIs. In the phase 2 UNICORN trial, we evaluated short-course preoperative botensilimab (BOT; multifunctional Fc-enhanced anti-CTLA-4 monoclonal antibody) alone or in combination with the anti-PD-1 monoclonal antibody balstilimab (BOT + BAL) in 56 patients with resectable, locally advanced CC. Twenty-eight patients with pMMR CC were sequentially enrolled in BOT (n = 14) and BOT + BAL (n = 14) cohorts. Twenty-eight patients with dMMR CC followed the same sequential allocation strategy. The primary endpoint of centrally assessed pathological major response (pMR) rate (≤10% of residual viable tumor) was met in all cohorts, except pMMR BOT. Specifically, the pMR rate was 0% (95% confidence interval (CI): 0-23.2%) in pMMR BOT, 36% (95% CI: 12.8-64.9%) in pMMR BOT + BAL, 36% (95% CI: 12.8-64.9%) in dMMR BOT and 100% (95% CI: 76.8-100%) in dMMR BOT + BAL. Secondary endpoints included safety, quality of life, describing treatment-induced transcriptional dynamics, peripheral blood mononuclear cell dynamics, radiomics and radiogenomics features, fecal microbiota composition and circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) dynamics. Eight (29%) and 15 (54%) patients treated with BOT and BOT + BAL, respectively, experienced immune-related adverse events, most commonly flu-like syndrome and diarrhea. Single-cell spatial transcriptomic analysis of matched baseline and post-treatment samples highlighted high baseline PD-L1 stromal expression and low post-treatment regulatory T cell signatures in pMMR responders, whereas dMMR responders displayed high baseline FCGR2A and FCGR3A expression on intratumoral macrophages. Clearance of ctDNA before surgery correlated with pathological response and lack of recurrence at data cutoff. Preoperative BOT + BAL elicits pathological responses in patients with pMMR or dMMR CC, supporting the combination as a promising strategy to expand ICI benefits to the early-stage setting. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT05845450 .

items.title: Perioperative ivonescimab with or without chemotherapy in resectable non-small cell lung cancer: a phase 2 trial
items.authors: Zhao X, Zhang B, Li C, et al.
items.abstract: Resectable non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) carries a high risk of postoperative recurrence, underscoring the need for effective perioperative therapies. This nonrandomized, noncomparative phase 2 trial evaluated neoadjuvant ivonescimab monotherapy (cohort 1) or in combination with chemotherapy (cohort 2), followed by surgery and adjuvant ivonescimab. In cohort 2, the major pathological response (MPR) rate was 70.1% (47/67; 95% confidence interval (CI) = 57.7-80.7); the lower bound of the 80% two-sided CI exceeded the historical control rate of 41% and the primary endpoint was met. The MPR rate in cohort 1 was 60.0% (6/10; 95% CI = 26.2-87.8). Among patients who achieved MPR, 83.3% (5/6) in cohort 1 and 97.9% (46/47) in cohort 2 had residual viable tumor (RVT) of ≤5%, respectively. Grade 3 or higher treatment-related adverse events (AEs) occurred in 36.4% (4/11) patients in cohort 1 and 30.4% (24/79) of those in cohort 2, with no grade 3 or higher hemorrhage or treatment-related death. Treatment-related surgery delay occurred in one (1.3%) patient. Surgery-related AEs related to ivonescimab occurred in 10.0% (1/10) and 10.4% (7/67) patients in the two cohorts, respectively, with no grade 3 or higher events reported. These data support perioperative ivonescimab with or without chemotherapy as a promising strategy for resectable NSCLC. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT05247684 .

items.title: Patient Communication and Radiation Safety in [(177)Lu]Lu-PSMA Radiopharmaceutical Therapy: International Survey of 102 Theranostic Centers
items.authors: Zahner J, Unterrainer LM, Czernin J, et al.
items.abstract: [177Lu]Lu-PSMA radiopharmaceutical therapy (RPT) is increasingly administered worldwide in both inpatient and outpatient settings. Despite its growing use, there is no harmonized international guidance on what patients should be told before, during, and after therapy. This study aimed to capture current clinical practice and expert opinion to identify areas of consensus and divergence to develop a patient information template. Methods: An international survey was conducted among theranostic centers performing [177Lu]Lu-PSMA RPT. The questionnaire covered pretreatment procedures, therapy procedures, radiation precautions guidance, and posttreatment procedures. Inpatient and outpatient settings were evaluated separately. Results: In total, 102 centers from 23 countries participated. High agreement was observed for most pretreatment procedures, core therapy aspects, and general posttreatment guidance. In contrast, substantial variability was identified in posttreatment radiation precautions, particularly regarding distancing measures, duration of precautions, transportation after discharge, household and hygiene recommendations, and guidance affecting social interactions. Conclusion: This international survey demonstrated broad consensus for core clinical procedures but showed variability in posttreatment radiation precautions after RPT. By summarizing current practice and translating it into a patient information template, this project supports more consistent patient guidance across diverse clinical settings.

items.title: Photobiomodulation for radiotherapy-induced dysgeusia in head and neck cancer patients: a pilot randomized clinical trial
items.authors: Viana PP, Pinto FC, Oliveira VB, et al.
items.abstract: Dysgeusia is a frequent complication in patients with head and neck cancer (HNC) undergoing radiotherapy and may negatively affect nutritional status and quality of life. This pilot study evaluated the effect of photobiomodulation (PBM) on the management of radiotherapy-induced dysgeusia. Sixteen patients undergoing radiotherapy for HNC were randomly assigned to either a PBM group (n = 8) or a zinc sulfate group (n = 8). Objective taste identification tests evaluating sweet, bitter, sour, and salty tastes were performed at three time points: before radiotherapy (T0), at the 15th radiotherapy session (T1), and at the 30th radiotherapy session (T2). Salty taste was the most affected taste modality in both groups. At T2, sweet taste was correctly identified by 75.0% of patients in the zinc group and 50.0% in the PBM group. In contrast, bitter taste was preserved in 87.5% of patients in the PBM group and 75.0% in the zinc group. Sour taste was preserved in 87.5% and 62.5% of patients in the PBM and zinc groups, respectively, whereas salty taste was preserved in 50.0% and 25.0% of patients, respectively. No statistically significant differences were observed between groups at T0, T1, or T2 (all p > 0.05). Although no statistically significant differences were identified, PBM was associated with better preservation of sour, bitter, and salty taste perception, particularly after the 30th radiotherapy session. These preliminary findings suggest that PBM may represent a promising supportive strategy for the management of treatment-related dysgeusia in patients with HNC undergoing radiotherapy.

items.title: Synergizing Short-Course Radiotherapy with Immunotherapy in Locally Advanced Rectal Cancer: Current Evidence, Challenges, and Future Directions
items.authors: Xu L, Jiao Y, Wei Y, et al.
items.abstract: The management of locally advanced rectal cancer is increasingly moving beyond a uniform cytotoxic framework toward biomarker-informed multimodal treatment. Short-course radiotherapy (SCRT) is an established and convenient radiotherapy option and may also provide an immunomodulatory context for immune checkpoint blockade. Preclinical evidence suggests that hypofractionated radiotherapy can promote immunogenic cell death and modulate the tumor immune microenvironment; however, whether the fractionation schedule of SCRT provides a clinically meaningful immunological advantage over long-course chemoradiotherapy remains uncertain. Early randomized studies of SCRT-based chemoimmunotherapy in predominantly proficient mismatch repair/microsatellite-stable (pMMR/MSS) populations have reported encouraging improvements in pathological or overall complete response rates compared with their respective control regimens. Nevertheless, differences in comparator arms, chemotherapy exposure, immunotherapy schedules, endpoint definitions, and follow-up duration preclude firm conclusions regarding the optimal radiotherapy backbone or long-term survival benefit. These findings support further prospective evaluation of SCRT-based combinations and response-adapted non-operative management in appropriately selected patients. Longitudinal circulating tumor DNA, multi-omics profiling, MR-guided adaptive radiotherapy, and computational models such as "digital twins" may contribute to improved patient selection and surveillance, but their clinical utility requires prospective validation.

items.title: RESPONSE-ADAPTIVE STEREOTACTIC BODY RADIOTHERAPY BOOST AFTER CONCURRENT CHEMORADIOTHERAPY IN UNRESECTABLE STAGE III NSCLC: A PROSPECTIVE SINGLE-CENTRE COHORT STUDY
items.journal: Int J Radiat Oncol Biol Phys
items.authors: Kiraz E, Eroğlu C, Gündoğ M, et al.
items.abstract: Objective: This study aimed to escalate the dose to the residual primary tumor with an adaptive stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) boost after concurrent chemoradiotherapy (CRT) in unresectable stage III non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), and to explore, within this cohort, whether a higher cumulative dose to the residual primary was associated with better locoregional control (LRC) and whether this translated into a difference in overall survival (OS). Materials And Methods: In this single-center, prospective, single-arm cohort, 51 patients received concurrent CRT (50 Gy/25 fractions with weekly carboplatin and paclitaxel) followed by an adaptive boost (30 Gy/5 fractions to the residual primary, 10 Gy/5 fractions to residual nodes), without consolidation durvalumab. Doses were summed by deformable registration and reported as EQD2. Response was assessed at 3 months with FDG-PET/CT (PERCIST), and toxicity with CTCAE v5.0. Outcomes estimated by Kaplan-Meier; predictors by Cox regression. Results: At a median follow-up of 26 months, 2-year OS and LRC were 61.5% and 62.8%. The median PFS and DMFS were 13 and 16 months, and distant metastasis was the dominant failure pattern (41.2%). Cumulative dose below 94.77 Gy (EQD2) to the residual primary independently predicted worse LRC (HR 5.86), and a 3-month locoregional SUVmax ≥4.55 predicted worse LRC (HR 5.04). OS was independently associated with residual nodal volume, 3-month metabolic progression, and subsequent locoregional progression. Grade 3-4 pneumonitis occurred in 7.8%, grade 3 esophagitis in one patient (2%), and hemoptysis in five (9.8%). Conclusion: The SBRT boost achieved encouraging locoregional control, including in bulky and node-advanced disease, without immunotherapy, and higher cumulative dose to the residual primary was associated with better locoregional control. Hemoptysis was the main safety concern and occurred predominantly in patients with pre-existing hemoptysis, supporting careful selection and strict bronchial constraints. Local escalation alone did not overcome the competing risk of distant failure.

items.title: Prevalence of Muscle loss during and after Pelvic Radiotherapy in Gynecological Cancer Patients
items.journal: Int J Radiat Oncol Biol Phys
items.authors: Laan JJ, Westerveld H, Hinnen KA, et al.
items.abstract: Introduction: Women undergoing pelvic radiotherapy are at risk of developing sarcopenia, defined by muscle loss. In patients treated with radiotherapy for cervical cancer, post-treatment muscle loss has been associated with poorer cancer-specific and overall survival. This study aimed to longitudinally assess sarcopenia and changes in muscle during radiotherapy and follow-up, and to evaluate whether bioelectrical impedance analysis can serve as an accurate bedside alternative to computed tomography (CT) for sarcopenia assessment. Methods And Materials: This prospective cohort study included women with histologically confirmed primary cervical, endometrial, vulvar, or vaginal cancer, all scheduled to undergo external beam radiotherapy (EBRT) with curative intent. Sarcopenia was assessed at baseline, during the last week of EBRT, and at the three- and six-month follow-up. Two methods were used to evaluate sarcopenia: lumbar skeletal muscle index measured via CT scan (gold standard) and appendicular skeletal muscle mass via bioelectrical impedance analysis. Fisher's exact test and the Mann-Whitney U test were used to compare baseline characteristics between women with and without sarcopenia during the last week of radiotherapy. Results: A total of 31 women were included. Based on CT scans, the prevalence of sarcopenia was 23% at baseline, 32% at the last week of radiotherapy, and 42% at the three-month follow-up. At the six-month follow-up, 29% of the women were sarcopenic. Bioelectrical impedance analysis detected sarcopenia in only 0% to 50% of cases across the various time points. Patients with FIGO stage III were significantly more frequently sarcopenic based on their appendicular skeletal muscle index as assessed by CT scan during the last week of EBRT. Conclusions: The prevalence of sarcopenia is high in women treated with radiotherapy for gynecological cancer. An increase in the prevalence of sarcopenia was observed, reaching its highest point at the three-month follow-up. Sarcopenia may be underestimated when assessed using bioelectrical impedance analysis, as indicated by the low sensitivity observed.

items.title: Pharmacotherapy for older adults with cancer: a digest of the Japanese clinical practice guidelines (2nd edition) - lung cancer
items.authors: Kubo T, Shimokata T, Tsukita Y, et al.
items.abstract: Background: The number of older adults with lung cancer is increasing in aging societies. However, determining optimal pharmacotherapy remains challenging because of heterogeneity in functional status, comorbidities, and the limited representation of older adults in clinical trials. Methods: This article presents an English digest of the second edition of the Japanese Clinical Practice Guidelines for Pharmacotherapy in Older Adults with Cancer, focusing on lung cancer. The guidelines were developed using the Minds 2020 methodology and incorporated systematic reviews, an evidence-to-decision framework, and multidisciplinary expert consensus. Results: These guidelines address key clinical questions in small-cell lung cancer (SCLC) and non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), including prophylactic cranial irradiation, adjuvant therapy, and immune checkpoint inhibitor-based treatments. Most recommendations were conditional, and no recommendation could be made for several clinical questions because of limited evidence in older populations. Prophylactic cranial irradiation may reduce brain metastases in selected patients with SCLC but requires careful consideration of potential neurocognitive toxicity. In resected NSCLC, tegafur-uracil may be an option for selected older patients; however, evidence supporting platinum-based chemotherapy and immunotherapy remains insufficient. In advanced NSCLC, immune checkpoint inhibitor monotherapy may benefit selected patients, whereas the role of chemoimmunotherapy remains uncertain because of insufficient age-specific evidence. Conclusions: These guidelines provide practical, evidence-based recommendations for pharmacotherapy in older adults with lung cancer. They emphasize individualized treatment strategies based on patient characteristics, treatment goals, and tolerability. Further research in older populations is required to strengthen the evidence base for geriatric oncology.
